name: Recursion
cs2023: SDF: Fundamental Programming Concepts and Practices
definition: Recursion is a technique in which a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller or simpler instance of the same problem. A correct recursive function has at least one base case that is answered directly without a recursive call, and recursive cases that make progress toward a base case. At runtime each call gets its own stack frame on the call stack, and each caller combines the results of its recursive calls after they return.

roles.name: Base case
roles.desc: An input small or simple enough to answer directly, with no recursive call; it stops the recursion.

roles.name: Recursive case
roles.desc: The branch where the function calls itself on a smaller or simpler version of the problem.

roles.name: Progress toward base case
roles.desc: The way each recursive call's input is strictly closer to a base case (e.g., n-1, a shorter list, half the range).

roles.name: Stack frame
roles.desc: The record created for one call, holding that call's own parameters, local variables, and where to resume after inner calls return.

roles.name: Call stack
roles.desc: The runtime stack of frames for all calls that have started but not yet returned.

roles.name: Return value / combining results
roles.desc: The value a call returns to its caller, which the caller uses to build its own result (e.g., n * factorial(n-1)).

relations.desc: Every chain of recursive calls must eventually reach a base case; if a base case is missing or never reached, the recursion is infinite and in practice ends with a stack overflow error (e.g., RecursionError in Python).
Each recursive case calls the function on an input strictly closer to a base case; a call on the same or a larger input (with respect to the base case) does not make progress.
Each call has its own stack frame with its own copies of parameters and local variables; assigning to a local variable in one call does not change the same-named variable in any other call.
A new frame is pushed onto the call stack for each call and popped when that call returns, so the most recently started call is always the first to finish (LIFO).
A base case returns a value without making any recursive call, and that value is the first one passed back up the chain of waiting calls.

A caller is suspended, not finished, while its recursive call runs; when the call returns, the caller resumes and uses the returned value to compute its own result, so results are combined on the way back up (unwinding).

misconceptions.wrong: A recursive call just jumps back to the top of the function like a loop, and the old call is gone.
misconceptions.correct: The calling instance is suspended with its frame kept on the call stack. When the inner call returns, the caller resumes right after the call and finishes its remaining work.

misconceptions.wrong: When the base case is reached, the recursion is over and the base case's value is the final answer.
misconceptions.correct: The base case returns only to its immediate caller. Each pending call then resumes and combines that value with its own work, and the final answer comes from the outermost call after the stack fully unwinds.

misconceptions.wrong: All the recursive calls share the same variables, so changing n in one call changes n everywhere.
misconceptions.correct: Each call has its own stack frame with separate parameters and locals. Only data that is explicitly shared (globals, or a mutable object passed by reference) is visible across calls.

misconceptions.wrong: As long as I write a base case somewhere, the recursion will stop.
misconceptions.correct: The recursive case must also make progress toward the base case on every path. For example, with base case n == 0, calling f(n - 2) from f(3) skips over 0 and recurses forever.

breaks_hint: Nested-doll or mirror-in-a-mirror images show self-similarity but usually omit the return trip, where each suspended call resumes and does more work with its inner call's result. Analogies that treat recursion as just going deeper also miss that each call keeps its own separate local state.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a base case in a recursive function?
choices: To make the function run faster
To handle an input directly, without recursion, so the chain of calls stops
To call the function again on a larger input
To store the results of every earlier call
quiz.explain: The base case is answered without a recursive call. Without a reachable base case, calls never stop and the stack overflows.

quiz.q: In a language without tail-call optimization, such as Python or Java, what happens on the call stack each time a recursive function calls itself?
choices: A new stack frame with its own parameters and local variables is pushed
The current frame is overwritten with the new arguments
Nothing; recursive calls do not use the call stack
quiz.explain: Every call gets a fresh frame on top of the call stack. Earlier frames stay there, suspended, until the calls above them return.
f(0) returns 0, then the waiting calls combine on the way back: f(1) = 1, f(2) = 3, f(3) = 6, f(4) = 10. 24 would be a product (factorial), not a sum.
g(3) calls g(1), then g(-1), g(-3), and so on; it skips over 0, so the base case is never reached. Even inputs like 4 and 10 reach 0.

choices: The student is right; the base case's value is the final answer
The student is wrong; the base case returns 1 to fact(2), which returns 2 to fact(3), which returns 6
The student is wrong; fact(3) returns 3 because only the first call multiplies
The student is wrong; fact(3) never reaches the base case
quiz.explain: The base case returns to its caller, not to the program. Each suspended call resumes and multiplies: fact(2) = 2 * 1 = 2, then fact(3) = 3 * 2 = 6.

generic_lesson:
Imagine sitting in a dark movie theater and wanting to know your row number. You can't see the signs, so you ask the person directly in front of you, "What row are you in?" That is the recursive case: you solve your problem by asking someone else the same, smaller question. They do the same thing, and the question passes forward one row at a time. Each step moves one row closer to the screen, which is the progress toward the base case.

The person in the front row needs to ask no one; they know they are in row 1. That is the base case, answered directly. They reply "1" to the person behind them, who adds one and answers "2," and so on back to you. Answers are combined on the way back, which is called unwinding.

While waiting, each person remembers their own question and what to do with the reply. In a program, that memory is a stack frame: every call has its own parameters and local variables, kept on the call stack. The most recent question is answered first. If the front row never answered, or the question were passed backward instead of forward, the waiting would never end; in code, that infinite recursion causes a stack overflow.
